newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian premier warns against poll complacency.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian premier warns against poll complacency.

text.p: Bulgaria's interim prime minister warned party colleagues on Tuesday not be complacent about winning a big enough majority in April 19 elections to carry on with vital economic reforms.

Stefan Sofianski, who returns to his former post as mayor of Sofia after the elections, said that in its two months in office his cabinet had halted bread and fuel shortages, secured a new reform and funding agreement with the IMF and laid the groundwork for a currency stabilisation programme.

But he said much remained to be done and the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), which is expected to form the next government, needed a stable parliamentary majority to pass necessary legislative measures.
"I hope we will achieve enough seats in parliament to be able to follow the policy of reforms, privatisation, the free market economy," Sofianski said.
"There are two weeks left and we have to work very hard."

The main parties have so far conducted a low-key campaign. The UDF, which led 30 days of mass nationwide protests against the former Socialist government in January and February, are confident of winning, and the Socialists expect to lose.
The political consensus painstakingly negotiated by President Petar Stoyanov in February is showing signs of unravelling as the elections approach.

Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov has withdrawn his support from the interim cabinet, accusing it of concealing the details of the IMF accord, and of sacking managers of state firms and government departments on political grounds.
Sofianski said the replacements were made for operational reasons, adding that the need for reform was self-evident. "If everything was OK, we wouldn't be in this situation now," he said.
After the Socialists agreed on February 4 to give up attempts to form a new government, Stoyanov dissolved parliament and appointed the cabinet led by Sofianski to govern until after the elections.
Some ministers, such as Deputy Prime Minister and Industry Minister Alexander Bozhkov, are expected to remain in the new government but others will be replaced.

One of the first tasks of the new administration will be to pass through parliament the draft 1997 budget and legislative changes to prepare for a currency board, a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime aimed at restoring confidence in the national currency.
Sofianski said he hoped to travel to Moscow at the end of the week to finalise an agreement on transiting Russian natural gas through Bulgaria, which would bring in significant revenue.
A Russian delegation is currently in Sofia and Sofianski said details on the amount of investments, the level of transit taxes and repayment methods still had to be settled.

A Bulgarian delegation is meeting the Group of 24 industrialised countries in Brussels on Tuesday and Wednesday to discuss additional support to accompany a standby accord agreed with the IMF last month.
Sofianski said the government was hoping for additional balance of payments support and a rescheduling of part of its $10 billion foreign debt.
